title: Alcohol dependence and withdrawal
blurb: Identify alcohol dependence, manage withdrawal safely and protect against seizures, delirium tremens and Wernicke's encephalopathy.
question: Mr Kowalski, 52, was admitted to an acute mental health ward last night with depression. He usually drinks a litre of vodka a day. This morning he is tremulous, sweating and anxious, and he walks unsteadily. Which action is the priority?

teach.body: In alcohol dependence the brain adapts to constant alcohol. Stop suddenly and it is left over-excited: tremor, sweating, anxiety, nausea, then in severe cases seizures and delirium tremens. NICE CG115 covers identifying and treating harmful drinking and dependence; CG100 covers acute withdrawal and Wernicke's encephalopathy. Plain English: for a dependent drinker, stopping is a medical event that needs planning, not willpower alone.

teach.caption: Standard teaching; timings vary. Assess on admission and monitor throughout with local protocol.

rows.label: Intake
values: Over 15 units a day, no red flags

teach.caption: Also consider inpatient at 15-30 units a day with significant comorbidity or cognitive impairment. Community: fixed-dose regimen over 7-10 days, reviewed every other day.
Often incomplete. NICE: maintain high suspicion, especially if intoxicated. Give parenteral thiamine for at least 5 days, then oral (CG100 1.2.1.4).

items: Oral thiamine for harmful or dependent drinkers who are malnourished, have decompensated liver disease, are in acute withdrawal or are about to start planned withdrawal.
Parenteral then oral thiamine if malnourished or with decompensated liver disease AND attending ED or admitted with acute illness or injury.
Suspected Wernicke's: parenteral thiamine (in the UK, Pabrinex) for at least 5 days unless excluded.
Dependent drinkers not admitted: advise against a sudden cut in intake and give support contacts (CG100 1.1.1.4).

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Kowalski on the ward
teach.body: About 12 hours after his last drink, Mr Kowalski shows withdrawal, and his unsteady gait raises the possibility of Wernicke's encephalopathy. The nurse escalates for immediate medical assessment, records observations and a CIWA-Ar score as an adjunct, and expects a benzodiazepine regimen (chlordiazepoxide or diazepam) and parenteral thiamine. He drinks well over 30 units a day, so close inpatient monitoring for seizures and delirium tremens is right.

teach.text: Phenytoin is NOT used for alcohol withdrawal seizures (CG100 1.1.5.3): use a quick-acting benzodiazepine such as lorazepam. And do not wait for all three Wernicke's signs: the triad is often incomplete, so treat on suspicion with parenteral thiamine.

items: AUDIT identifies; SADQ rates dependence; CIWA-Ar rates withdrawal.
Inpatient withdrawal: over 30 units a day, SADQ over 30, past seizures or DTs, or benzodiazepine co-dependence.
Chlordiazepoxide or diazepam; lorazepam in liver impairment and for DTs; no phenytoin for withdrawal seizures.
Suspected Wernicke's: parenteral thiamine for at least 5 days, then oral.

summary: You can now use AUDIT, SADQ and CIWA-Ar, decide where withdrawal should happen and choose the NICE drugs for withdrawal, delirium tremens and seizures. You can also recognise Wernicke's encephalopathy and give thiamine correctly.

A.q: Which tool does NICE CG115 name for measuring the severity of alcohol dependence?
A.why: CG115 names the SADQ (or LDQ) for severity of dependence; AUDIT identifies and CIWA-Ar rates withdrawal.

whyNot.0: CIWA-Ar measures the severity of withdrawal, not dependence.
whyNot.1: AUDIT is for identification and as an outcome measure.
whyNot.3: CAGE is not one of the tools CG115 names.

A.q: Which drug does NICE CG100 recommend first line for delirium tremens?
options: Oral chlordiazepoxide at a fixed dose
A.why: CG100 1.1.4.1: offer oral lorazepam first line for delirium tremens; parenteral lorazepam or haloperidol if symptoms persist or oral medicine is declined.

whyNot.1: Phenytoin is not used in alcohol withdrawal complications.
whyNot.2: CG100 1.1.4.1 names oral lorazepam, not chlordiazepoxide, as first line once delirium tremens has developed; any existing withdrawal regimen is reviewed (1.1.4.2).
whyNot.3: Olanzapine is not the CG100 choice; haloperidol is the named antipsychotic.

A.q: A dependent drinker has liver impairment and needs assisted withdrawal. Which benzodiazepine does NICE CG115 suggest considering?
options: Diazepam at the usual starting dose
A.why: CG115 1.3.5.10: in liver impairment consider a benzodiazepine needing limited liver metabolism, such as lorazepam, starting with a reduced dose and monitoring liver function.

whyNot.0: Diazepam relies on liver metabolism; doses need reducing in liver impairment.
whyNot.1: Higher doses of a long-acting drug risk accumulation.
whyNot.2: Clomethiazole is not offered for community withdrawal because of overdose and misuse risk.

B.q: Mr Hughes, dependent on alcohol, has an alcohol withdrawal seizure on the ward. What does NICE CG100 recommend to reduce the chance of further seizures?
options: Start an intravenous phenytoin loading dose
A quick-acting benzodiazepine such as lorazepam
Start sodium valproate by mouth twice daily
B.why: CG100 1.1.5.1: consider a quick-acting benzodiazepine such as lorazepam; 1.1.5.3: do not offer phenytoin for alcohol withdrawal seizures.

whyNot.0: CG100 specifically advises against phenytoin here.
whyNot.2: Glucose treats hypoglycaemia; it does not prevent withdrawal seizures.
whyNot.3: Valproate is not the CG100 treatment for withdrawal seizures.

B.q: Ms Doyle drinks about 35 units a day and had delirium tremens during a previous detox. She wants to withdraw at home. What does NICE CG115 suggest?
options: Stop drinking abruptly with family support
Reduce drinking by half before any review
B.why: CG115 1.3.4.5: consider inpatient or residential withdrawal for people drinking over 30 units a day or with a history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens.

whyNot.0: Community withdrawal suits people without these risk factors.
whyNot.1: Sudden cessation can cause severe withdrawal in dependent drinkers.
whyNot.3: This delays a safe, supervised plan.

B.q: A harmful drinker who is malnourished attends the emergency department with a fall. What thiamine does NICE CG100 recommend?
options: Oral thiamine on discharge from the department
No thiamine unless he is in withdrawal
Thiamine after his first meal on the ward
Parenteral thiamine followed by oral thiamine
B.why: CG100 1.2.1.3: offer prophylactic parenteral thiamine followed by oral thiamine to harmful or dependent drinkers who are malnourished (or at risk) or have decompensated liver disease and attend ED or are admitted.

whyNot.0: Malnourishment plus attending ED means parenteral thiamine first.
whyNot.2: Thiamine should not wait for a meal.

C.q: Day 2 of admission: Mr Kowalski is newly confused, cannot walk without help and has jerky eye movements. His withdrawal score is improving. What is the most likely problem and priority?
options: Oversedation; withhold the next dose and observe
Worsening depression; refer to the psychiatrist
C.why: Confusion, ataxia and nystagmus suggest Wernicke's encephalopathy; CG100 1.2.1.4: give parenteral thiamine for at least 5 days unless excluded, then oral.

whyNot.0: Improving withdrawal scores with ataxia and eye signs point to Wernicke's, and haloperidol is not first line for DTs.
whyNot.2: Oversedation does not explain new nystagmus and ataxia.
whyNot.3: These are neurological signs needing urgent physical treatment.

C.q: Jake, 16, is admitted in acute alcohol withdrawal. What does NICE CG100 say about where he should be managed?
options: Community withdrawal with daily nurse visits
Outpatient review by CAMHS within the next 2 weeks
Consider a lower threshold for hospital admission
Home withdrawal supervised by a parent
C.why: CG100 1.1.1.3: for vulnerable groups including people aged 16 or 17, consider a lower threshold for hospital admission for medically assisted withdrawal (under-16s are offered admission, 1.1.1.2).

whyNot.0: Young age lowers the threshold for admission.
whyNot.1: Acute withdrawal needs medical management now.
whyNot.3: Home withdrawal is not the NICE approach for a vulnerable 16-year-old in acute withdrawal.

C.q: After a successful assisted withdrawal, Mrs Lane, moderately dependent, wants help to stay abstinent. Which option fits NICE CG115?
options: Acamprosate or naltrexone with psychological therapy
Disulfiram as the first choice for everyone
Diazepam at a low maintenance dose for 6 months
Acamprosate started once 6 months abstinent from alcohol
C.why: CG115 1.3.6.1: after a successful withdrawal for moderate and severe dependence, consider acamprosate or oral naltrexone combined with an individual psychological intervention; disulfiram (1.3.6.3) if these are unsuitable or the person prefers it.

whyNot.1: Disulfiram is for when acamprosate and naltrexone are unsuitable or preferred.
whyNot.2: Long-term benzodiazepines are not relapse prevention.
whyNot.3: Acamprosate should start as soon as possible after withdrawal.

reteach.title: Settle the withdrawal, protect the brain
reteach.question: What are the two jobs in every alcohol withdrawal?

blocks.body: Job one: calm the over-excited brain with a benzodiazepine (chlordiazepoxide or diazepam; lorazepam if the liver is impaired or for delirium tremens). Job two: protect the brain from thiamine deficiency, with parenteral thiamine when Wernicke's is suspected or when malnourished drinkers come to ED or are admitted.

blocks.text: Seizure in withdrawal: lorazepam, not phenytoin.

explain.body: AUDIT identifies risky drinking (over 15: comprehensive assessment by specialist services). SADQ or LDQ measures dependence. CIWA-Ar measures withdrawal.

test.q: An adult referred to specialist alcohol services scores 18 on the AUDIT. What does NICE CG115 suggest?
options: Brief advice and discharge to the GP
Admission for withdrawal the same day
test.why: CG115 1.2.2.6: consider a comprehensive assessment for adults referred to specialist alcohol services who score more than 15 on the AUDIT.

whyNot.0: A score over 15 calls for fuller assessment.
whyNot.2: The setting for withdrawal follows assessment of dependence and risk.

explain.body: Consider inpatient withdrawal at over 30 units a day, SADQ over 30, previous seizures or DTs, epilepsy, or benzodiazepine co-dependence. Community programmes use a fixed-dose regimen over 7-10 days.

test.q: Which finding makes NICE CG115 suggest considering inpatient rather than community alcohol withdrawal?
options: Drinking 20 units a day with no other problems
A partner willing to supervise doses
test.why: CG115 1.3.4.5: a SADQ score of more than 30 is a criterion for considering inpatient or residential withdrawal.

whyNot.0: 15-30 units a day needs added comorbidity to meet the criteria.
whyNot.2: AUDIT 12 does not meet the inpatient criteria.
whyNot.3: A supervising partner supports community withdrawal.

explain.body: Chlordiazepoxide or diazepam for planned withdrawal; lorazepam in liver impairment; oral lorazepam for DTs; quick-acting benzodiazepine for seizures; no phenytoin; no clomethiazole in the community.

test.q: Which drug does NICE CG115 name as preferred for a planned assisted alcohol withdrawal?
test.why: CG115 1.3.5.3: the preferred medication for assisted withdrawal is a benzodiazepine, chlordiazepoxide or diazepam.

whyNot.1: Haloperidol is an option for delirium tremens, not planned withdrawal.
whyNot.2: Carbamazepine is an alternative in CG100, not the CG115 preferred drug.
whyNot.3: Clomethiazole carries overdose and misuse risk and is not for community use.

explain.body: Confusion, ataxia, eye signs; often incomplete. High suspicion, especially when intoxicated. Parenteral thiamine for at least 5 days, then oral.

test.q: For suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy, how long does NICE CG100 advise giving parenteral thiamine unless the diagnosis is excluded?
test.why: CG100 1.2.1.4: parenteral thiamine for a minimum of 5 days unless Wernicke's encephalopathy is excluded, followed by oral thiamine.

whyNot.1: 48 hours is shorter than the CG100 minimum.
whyNot.3: Duration is set by CG100, not by appetite.
